newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico's Cetes rates drop again, but demand slumps.
newsitem.headline: Mexico's Cetes rates drop again, but demand slumps.

text.p: Mexico's Treasury bill rates fell across the board for the ninth consecutive week on Tuesday, but analysts warned that slumping demand could signal that rates have hit a short-term floor.
Rates on benchmark one-month paper fell 23 basis points to 19.46 percent, a new post-devaluation low, while rates in longer terms fell slightly more.

Rates did not drop as much as expected in the 28- or 182-day paper but fell more than thought in the three-month and one-year Cetes. A Reuters survey of local dealers earlier on Tuesday forecast a fall of 52 basis points in the 28-day paper.

"The short-term rate did not fall as much as expected, so that could mean this downward spiral (in rates) is coming to an end -- that rates have hit a floor," said Francisco Gutierrez, director of analysis at Inverlat Brokerage in Mexico City.
Because some rates fell more than expected and others less, the country's financial markets may interpret the net effect of the auction as neutral, according to MMS International.
"Markets may have already priced in the lower rates and this may not have an effect on the peso," MMS said in a market commentary.
But falling demand could be a sign that investors are finding returns in Mexican T-bills less and less attractive. Demand fell to 8.95 billion pesos from 13.36 billion last week.

Other analysts noted that higher real rates in longer terms were driving investors toward the long end of the curve, a move that could lead them to abandon the market next time around if they feel they have soaked up all the value.

"We are starting to see a more definitive move toward the long end of the curve, a sign the market may be over-bought or tiring and a risk of correction," said Gene Frieda, an analyst at I.D.E.A. in New York.

Frieda and others agreed, however, that predicting a correction was difficult because rates could continue to decline as long as the peso remained steady. And a steady peso prompts more dollars to enter Mexico in search of higher returns.
"During December and January, the foreign investor has gotten great returns on Cetes because the nominal return in pesos has been the same as the nominal return in dollars," Gutierrez said.

He said he would like to see the peso begin to weaken, a move that would cause rates to rise slightly but would prevent any significant deterioration in Mexico's external finances and bring on a more extreme correction in rates and the peso later.
"Rates at this point are even ahead of inflation, and over the long-run that is unhealthy," he said.
Frieda said that while he would also welcome a slight correction in rates, low U.S. long-term interest rates may continue to force investors into emerging markets and help to bouy the peso.
